title: Roots first: the growth you cannot see yet
description: A seedling that looks stalled may be doing its most important work underground. Plants build roots before they build height — and the same order quietly governs skills, habits and confidence.

body.heading: Underground comes first
paragraphs: A young plant's first organ is not a leaf but a root, driving down before anything green appears. Gardeners know the pattern so well they have a saying for the first seasons of a perennial: sleep, creep, leap. Year one looks like nothing; the plant is building the hidden system that year three's drama will stand on.

Roots do the unglamorous essentials: anchoring against storms, finding water in dry weeks, storing food for hard times. A plant pushed to grow tall before it grows deep is not advanced — it is fragile, and the first drought grades it honestly.

body.heading: Your version of root work
paragraphs: Learning works the same way. The weeks where a language, an instrument or a craft feels stuck are often root weeks: vocabulary settling in, fingers memorising, judgement quietly forming below the level where you can watch it. The progress is real; it is just not yet visible from above ground.

Root work has a recognisable texture — repetition without applause, basics practised past boredom, questions you cannot yet phrase properly. If your practice feels like that right now, it may not be failing. It may be rooting.

body.heading: Judge by the season, not the day
paragraphs: Gardeners do not dig up a seed to check on it, because the checking kills the growing. Give your own root work the same protection: measure monthly, not daily, and look for root-signs — things slightly easier, slightly faster, slightly less frightening than last month.
Then, when the leap comes, it will look sudden to everyone except you. You will know exactly how long it was underground.

takeaway: Plants build roots before height, and learners do too: judge quiet, repetitive progress by the month, not the day — the leap is grown underground.
